newsitem.title: USA: Lawsuit may give New Jersey taxpayers a break.
newsitem.headline: Lawsuit may give New Jersey taxpayers a break.

text.p: Colonial Mutual Funds said Monday it and the Investment Company Institute won a tax court lawsuit that could mean tax refunds for some New Jersey residents who invest in mutual funds. The Tax Court of New Jersey ruled on Feb. 21 that New Jersey should not have required mutual fund investors to pay taxes on interest income earned from U.S. debt securities, regardless of the proportion of those securities contained in mutual funds, Colonial said. "We entered this case in 1993 because we believed the income from these investments should be tax-free in all cases," Colonial Chief Executive Stephen Gibson said in a statement. "This decision represents a victory for taxpayers..."

A spokeswoman for the New Jersey Department of Treasury said the state is still deciding whether to appeal the decision and calculating how much the verdict could cost the state. "We still are looking over the decision," spokeswoman Mary Lou Murphy told Reuters. "At this point, the division is not expecting any huge refund exposure."
Earlier in the case, New Jersey had estimated that millions of dollars could be affected by the decision, Colonial said.
New Jersey had taxed income from U.S. debt securities contained in mutual funds that had less than 80 percent of their investments in those securities, Boston-based Colonial said.

The state did allow investors in mutual funds with more than 80 percent of their assets in U.S. government securities to exempt the income that was derived from those securities from state taxes, the company said.

Colonial advised New Jersey residents who think they might be affected by the decision to apply for a refund. With a three-year statute of limitations, New Jersey taxpayers could receive a refund as far back as 1993 if they filed amended state income tax returns by April 15, Colonial said. "We'll do everything we can to make sure the affected taxpayers are aware that they may qualify for a refund," Gibson said. Three states, California, Connecticut and New York, still impose some requirements before mutual funds can qualify for state tax exemptions, Colonial said. ((Boston office, (617) 367-4106))
